about: The Lord's Prayer, which Jesus taught His disciples (Mt 6:9–13, and in a shorter form at Lk 11:2–4). It addresses God as Father. It asks that His name be hallowed, His kingdom come, and His will be done, and then asks for daily bread, forgiveness, not to be led into temptation, and deliverance from evil.

seg.tr: Our Father, who art in heaven,

ex.w006: Latin has plural “cælis” here and singular “cælo” later. The received English says “heaven” in both places.

seg.tr: Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven.

ex.w013: The same form “fiat” occurs in Mary's reply at the Annunciation (Lk 1:38).

seg.tr: Give us this day our daily bread.

ex.w022: Latin says literally “give us our bread”. The received English preserves the same direct object.

seg.tr: And forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us.

ex.w037: Literally: debtors, those who owe us something. The received English speaks of those who trespass against us.

seg.tr: And lead us not into temptation,

ex.w042: The received English combines the two as “lead us not”.

seg.tr: but deliver us from evil. Amen.

ex.w046: “Líbera” means “deliver”, the wording retained by the familiar English prayer.
ex.w049: This edition parses “malo” as the neuter noun for evil. The Mass embolism takes it up in the neuter plural, “ab ómnibus malis.” The Catechism also explains that the petition ultimately refers to the Evil One (CCC 2851).

nt.w049: The form is the ablative of both words at once. It can be malum, evil as a thing, or malus, the Evil One. Neither the form nor the sentence decides, and the tradition reads it both ways. This edition takes malum and marks the doubt.
